lessonRef.title: Discussion or presentation practice: presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately within the unit “Narrative Craft, Comparison, and the Year-End Portfolio.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's discussion or presentation practice work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
In September I thought revising meant fixing spelling.

I would write a paragraph, read it once for red underlines, and call it finished. When my teacher wrote *develop this* in the margin, I genuinely did not know what she was asking for. The sentence was correct. What else was there?

The answer arrived in November, and it arrived through a piece I did not care about.

We had to explain a process. I chose how a lock works on a canal, because my uncle had shown me one. I wrote four sentences. My partner read them and asked why the water does not simply run out the bottom. I said because of the gates. She asked how the gates hold back that much water. I said because they are strong. She said that was not an answer, and she was right, and I was annoyed for about a day.

Then I went and found out. The gates form a shallow V pointing upstream, so the water pressure pushes them together instead of apart. The harder the water pushes, the tighter they seal.

When I put that in, the paragraph stopped being four correct sentences and started being something a person could learn from.

That is what *develop this* meant. It took me two months and one annoying question to find out.

In March I wrote an opinion piece and someone asked me a question I could not answer, and I recognized the feeling immediately. I did not get annoyed. I went and found out.

I still misspell *necessary*. I expect I always will. But I no longer think that is what revising is.

refs.title: What the Year Taught Me
refs.author: Manuel Academy
refs.rightsStatement: Original Manuel Academy instructional text. Included in full for enrolled learner course use.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “What the Year Taught Me”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “What the Year Taught Me,” then answer: What is the most defensible claim about presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately that a careful reader could debate after reading this source?

Deliverable: Grade 4: a discussion brief with a claim, evidence, and a fair response to another view; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately is not yet secure, return to “What the Year Taught Me” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply presenting one portfolio piece in an organized way, or privately to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “What the Year Taught Me.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
